afrobeat.hook: Fela Kuti's mix of highlife and jazz did not sell in Lagos. On a 1969 trip to the United States a former Black Panther gave him Malcolm X to read, and he came to see that he had not been playing African music. Talking Heads later carried Afrobeat's polyrhythms into Remain in Light.

beats.why: She gave him the writings of Martin Luther King Jr., Angela Davis and, above all, Malcolm X. Kuti came to see that he had not been playing African music. The new music drew on highlife, fuji and jùjú. The name Afrobeat was meant partly to set it apart from the soul of James Brown.
beats.after: Brian Eno and David Byrne carried its polyrhythms into Talking Heads' 1980 album Remain in Light. Kuti's sons Femi and Seun play it today.

afrobeats.hook: The name is credited to the London-based DJ Abrantee, who added an s to Fela Kuti's afrobeat to present the sound to British dancefloors. Afroswing grew out of it in the UK, and in 2016 Drake released "One Dance" with Wizkid.

amapiano.hook: Nobody agrees who started amapiano or in which South African township. What is agreed is the sound: piano melodies over a log-drum bass that one producer is credited with finding while trying out new plug-ins. In 2023 Tyla's "Water" took it into the US Billboard Hot 100.

beats.before: Amapiano mixes kwaito, deep house, gqom, jazz, soul and lounge music. In the 2000s DJ Spoko, who had moved to Atteridgeville west of Pretoria, DJ Mujava and others made bacardi house, known as sgubhu saPitori.
beats.who: Because amapiano resembles bacardi house, some place its start in Pretoria, but accounts from the Johannesburg townships differ and no single founder is agreed.
beats.why: The name is the Zulu word for "pianos", and the music is built on piano melodies and log-drum basslines. MDU aka TRP is credited with finding the log-drum sound while trying out new plug-ins.
beats.after: Young people posted dance videos set to it on social media, which fed the dance scene in South Africa. In 2019 it spread across Africa, and in 2022 the online store Beatport gave it its own charts. In 2023 Tyla's "Water" became the first song by a South African soloist to enter the US Billboard Hot 100 in 55 years.

baroque.hook: In late Renaissance Florence a circle of humanists and musicians rejected the many-voiced polyphony of their day and looked to ancient Greek drama; the earliest opera that survives is from 1600. In 1637 Venice opened Europe's first public opera house.

beats.who: In 1598 Jacopo Peri and the poet Ottavio Rinuccini staged Dafne, sung throughout, and in 1600 Peri's Euridice followed, the earliest surviving opera.
beats.why: The accompaniment was a figured bass: a keyboard player read figures written above the bass line and improvised the chords. blues.hook: The blues became a genre of its own as Black families left the Southern countryside for the cities in the 1920s. Chicago became a centre of electric blues from 1948, when Muddy Waters, born in Mississippi, recorded "I Can't Be Satisfied", and the blues went on into rhythm and blues.

bolero.hook: Pepe Sánchez of Santiago de Cuba wrote the first bolero in 1883 and never wrote a song down, so most of his are lost. Radio carried the bolero to Puerto Rico and Mexico, and mixed with son it became the ballroom rhumba in the United States.

beats.before: The bolero did not stem directly from the Italian opera and canzone then popular in Havana, but from romantic folk poetry sung by a new kind of troubadour in Santiago de Cuba, the trovadores. These itinerant musicians travelled around Oriente province and earned their living by singing and playing the guitar.

bossa.hook: João Gilberto cut a whole samba drum band down to one guitar: his thumb played the bass drum's part, his fingers the tamborim's. Three years after his 1959 LP, bossa nova was at Carnegie Hall, and in 1964 his album with Stan Getz won Grammy Awards.

beats.after: On 21 November 1962 Brazil's consulate presented bossa nova at Carnegie Hall in New York. carnatic.hook: South India's classical music is still traditionally taught by the system Purandara Dasa formulated in the 16th century. Its violin came from Fort St. George, where the composer Dikshitar and his brothers heard Western orchestral music and one brother brought the instrument in.

beats.after: When the princely states dissolved around independence in 1947, patronage passed to private societies called sabhas that sold tickets to concerts.

cumbia.hook: Cumbia began on Colombia's Caribbean coast as a dance to drums and flutes, with no singing at all. Record companies on the coast carried it abroad from the 1940s, and by the 1960s bands in Peru were leading it with electric guitars.

beats.who: In Barranquilla in 1888 a woman known as La Cañón set up large cumbiamba circles at the four corners of Bolívar street, danced to drums and flutes.
beats.why: Cumbia had been instrumental; in time, singers were added. Clarinetist Lucho Bermúdez, who grew up in El Carmen de Bolívar, wrote stylized orchestral arrangements of cumbia, and by the 1940s it was spreading from the coast to the rest of Colombia. Record companies on the coast, among them Discos Fuentes, founded in 1934, helped carry it abroad.
beats.after: In Mexico in the 1940s the Colombian singer Luis Carlos Meyer and orchestra director Rafael de Paz made La Cumbia Cienaguera, considered the first cumbia recorded outside Colombia. In 1960s Peru, Los Destellos were among the first to lead cumbia with electric guitars.

dancehall.hook: The 1985 hit "Under Mi Sleng Teng" was built on the "rock" preset of a small Casio keyboard, because one of its makers could not afford a Yamaha. Many artists recorded over the same rhythm track, and dancehall's faster electronic beat shaped Spanish-language reggae.

beats.before: Dancehall began in the late 1970s among working-class people in inner-city Kingston who could not go to dances uptown. As Edward Seaga's government replaced Michael Manley's, music moved away from internationally oriented roots reggae toward local listeners.
beats.why: Radio would not play it, so it spread through sound systems and record dealers. Deejays toasted over rhythm tracks from 1960s and 1970s reggae. In 1984 Wayne Smith and Noel Davey built a riddim on the "rock" preset of a Casiotone MT-40 keyboard, because Davey could not afford a Yamaha DX-7. King Jammy released it as "Under Mi Sleng Teng" in 1985, and many artists recorded over the same riddim.
beats.after: Shabba Ranks won a Grammy for his 1991 album As Raw as Ever, and dancehall's faster electronic beat shaped Reggae en Español.

disco.hook: Disco grew at private parties in Manhattan where gay men, often harassed in bars, could dance together without fear of the police. Its DJs mixed one record into the next so the dancing never stopped, and one of them, Frankie Knuckles, went on to help develop house.

beats.before: In Philadelphia in the early 1970s, the producers Gamble and Huff gave soul lush strings, thumping basslines and sliding hi-hats.
beats.who: On Valentine's Day 1970 the DJ David Mancuso held his first major party at his Manhattan home, later called the Loft.
beats.why: Gay men, often harassed in bars, could dance there together without fear of the police. DJs mixed one record into the next with no break, so the dancing never stopped.
beats.after: The films Saturday Night Fever (1977) and Thank God It's Friday (1978) took it into the mainstream. In the United States it declined after Disco Demolition Night on 12 July 1979. Frankie Knuckles, a disco DJ, went on to help develop house music in the 1980s.

edmpop.hook: From 2009 the Paris DJ David Guetta made hits with pop and hip-hop singers, and acts such as Avicii and Swedish House Mafia toured arenas, not clubs; in 2011 Swedish House Mafia sold out Madison Square Garden. The American industry called it EDM, and in 2016 Guetta released a single called "The Death of EDM".

frenchhouse.hook: In mid-1990s France, producers who were also DJs built house tracks from samples and filtered loops, and Daft Punk's Homework reached the UK top 10. Stardust's "Music Sounds Better with You" sold over two million copies, and Madonna drew on the sound in 2005.

gagaku.hook: Japan's court set up a bureau for this music in 701, and descendants of its guild musicians still make up most of the Imperial Palace Music Department. It began as an import: music from Tang China and Korea that fused with native song in the 9th and 10th centuries.

gregorian.hook: Gregorian chant spread because Charlemagne pushed it through his empire to consolidate his power, and by the 9th century it had replaced the local chant of Gaul. The signs invented to show singers the shape of its melodies grew into modern staff notation.

hindustani.hook: North India's classical music took shape in the courts of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, where Hindu and Muslim ideas met in new forms such as khyal and qawwali. When the Mughal Empire broke up, the styles kept at smaller courts became the gharanas.

house.hook: In Chicago, dance music passed from major labels to DJs in underground clubs, where Frankie Knuckles mixed records together and added a drum machine for dancers who were mainly black gay men. In 1987 a Chicago house record was number one in Britain.

beats.before: In Chicago, dance music passed from major labels to DJs in the underground clubs.
beats.who: Frankie Knuckles, who had moved from New York City, was resident DJ at the Warehouse in Chicago from 1977 to 1982, where the dancers were mainly black gay men.
beats.why: Knuckles mixed songs together instead of playing records one after another, and added a drum machine and a reel-to-reel tape player to make new tracks. By one account, the Importes Etc. record shop labelled his records "As Heard at the Warehouse", shortened to "House". In 1984 Jesse Saunders made "On and On" with a Roland TR-808 drum machine and a TB-303 bass synthesizer. From 1985 more Chicago DJs released their own tracks on newly affordable electronic instruments, for clubs serving mainly black, Mexican American and gay audiences.
beats.after: In January 1987 Steve "Silk" Hurley's "Jack Your Body" reached number one in the UK, and Britain had its Second Summer of Love in 1988 and 1989.

jpop.hook: The word J-pop came from a Tokyo radio station that at first played no Japanese music and chose a "J" to label the Japanese records it let in around 1989. Ten years later Hikaru Utada's First Love became the best-selling album in Oricon chart history.

beats.who: The new name came from J-Wave, a radio station in Roppongi that opened on 1 October 1988 and at first played no Japanese music. beats.after: Japan's physical music sales peaked in 1998, and Hikaru Utada's first Japanese album, First Love, released in March 1999, became the best-selling album in Oricon history.

beats.before: Mariachi grew out of the son jalisciense, the string music of the Jalisco area. Its early players used only string instruments such as guitars and harps and dressed in peasant clothes.
beats.who: Most sources place its birth in the town of Cocula, Jalisco, in the 19th century. In 1905 a hacienda family brought a mariachi from Cocula to Mexico City to play for President Porfirio Díaz.

melodic.hook: After his mother died and his engagement ended, Kanye West felt rapping could not carry what he felt. He mostly sang, through Auto-Tune, over an 808 drum machine, and rappers mocked him. The album is credited with starting emo rap.

metal.hook: Tony Iommi lost the ends of two fingers in a work accident, so he tuned his guitar down and leaned on power chords, which were easier to finger. Black Sabbath's first album in 1970 is taken as the first heavy metal record, and American bands later built thrash from the style.

beats.who: Lex Luger, born in 1991, drummed in church bands, made beats on an unlicensed copy of FL Studio and from late 2008 posted them on Myspace. In 2009 the rapper Waka Flocka Flame wrote back, and later flew him to Atlanta.
beats.why: Luger produced most of Waka's album Flockaveli (5 October 2010): 808 trills, bass kicks, hand claps, dense synthesizers and shifting sub-bass layers under constant ad-libs.
beats.after: In Chicago, Chief Keef's "I Don't Like" and "Love Sosa" spawned drill as a subgenre of trap. Katy Perry's "Dark Horse" with Juicy J reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 2014.

reggae.hook: In 1968 a Kingston engineer left the vocal off a record by accident, and the sound-system operator who had ordered it kept the result. Five years later Lee "Scratch" Perry released Blackboard Jungle Dub, and British reggae went on to feed drum and bass and dubstep.

reggaeton.hook: In 1995 police in San Juan raided six record stores and seized reggaeton cassettes under obscenity laws; the music was first sung in housing projects and sold from car trunks. rocknroll.hook: A Cleveland disc jockey began calling sped-up rhythm and blues "rock and roll" in 1951, and it developed as a genre of its own once it was realised that affluent white teenagers were listening. On April 12, 1954, Bill Haley & His Comets recorded "Rock Around the Clock". In July 1954 Elvis Presley recorded "That's All Right" at Sam Phillips' Sun Studio in Memphis. Chuck Berry, drawing on electric blues, made the electric guitar its centrepiece.

romantic.hook: Composers had lived on aristocratic patronage; in the 19th century they often wrote for public concerts with large paying audiences. Wagner took chromatic harmony to its extreme, and Schoenberg and Debussy answered as Romanticism came apart.

beats.before: In 1810 E. T. A. Hoffmann reviewed Beethoven's Fifth Symphony and set out the principles of musical Romanticism, holding instrumental music to be the art best suited to expressing emotion. Composers had lived under aristocratic patronage; now they often wrote for public concerts with large paying audiences.
beats.who: The move away from Viennese classicism ran through the work of Beethoven and of Franz Schubert, one of the first composers of Romantic lieder, as in Erlkönig.
beats.after: Richard Wagner took chromatic harmony to its extreme in Tristan und Isolde, and from 1876 the Bayreuth Festival staged only his works. rumbacongo.hook: In the early 1940s Radio Congo Belge in Léopoldville played records of Cuban son, and Congolese musicians moved its piano, drum and trumpet parts onto electric guitars and saxophones. The imported records were often labelled "rumba", so the new music took that name, and soukous grew out of it.

beats.who: Wendo Kolosoy's "Marie-Louise", written with the guitarist Henri Bowane for the Ngoma label, sold over two million copies. Request logs from 1954 show 30,000 music requests, 90% of them for Congolese rumba songs.
beats.why: Congolese musicians moved the piano parts, drum patterns and trumpet phrases of son onto electric guitars and saxophones. Because the imported records were often labelled "rumba", the local music took that name. Antoine Kasongo's orchestra is credited with adding the sebene, a repeated instrumental passage built on guitar figures.
beats.after: In the 1960s and 1970s soukous grew out of it. In the 1980s many musicians left Zaire for Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Colombia, and for Paris, Brussels and London.

samba.hook: Urban samba grew at gatherings in the homes of Bahian women who had moved to Rio after slavery was abolished. Musicians organised the first samba schools to avoid police harassment, in the 1930s it was Brazil's most recorded genre, and bossa nova later came from it.

beats.before: Rio's urban samba drew on rural traditions from across Brazil. After slavery was abolished, Black Bahians moved to Rio in growing numbers.
beats.who: Women from Bahia, the "Tias Baianas", founded the city's first Candomblé terreiros. Their homes held cooking and the gatherings called pagodes, where urban samba grew. "Pelo Telefone", released on 19 January 1917, was a hit at that year's Rio carnival. Donga registered it under his name, and contemporaries said he had taken a collective song.
beats.why: Musicians in the Estácio neighbourhood made a samba with a faster tempo and longer notes. To avoid police harassment, they organised themselves into what they called samba schools.
beats.after: Between 1931 and 1940 samba was the most recorded genre in Brazil. Later, a new way of accompanying and singing samba, spread from Rio's South Zone, became known as bossa nova.

ska.hook: When new American rhythm and blues records ran short in the late 1950s, Jamaica's sound-system owners began recording local artists, and within two or three years the copied shuffle had become ska. It slowed into rocksteady, and bands around Coventry later joined it to punk guitar.

beats.before: After the Second World War, Jamaicans bought radios and could hear rhythm and blues from the American South. Ska joined that sound to Caribbean mento and American jazz.
beats.who: To meet the demand, Prince Buster, Coxsone Dodd and Duke Reid set up sound systems. In the second half of 1959 Dodd and Reid began issuing their own recordings of local artists on disc. Its rise coincided with Jamaica's independence from Britain in 1962.
beats.why: The producers had turned to recording local artists because new American jump blues and R&B tunes ran short in the late 1950s. Within two or three years the copied American shuffle had become ska, with the guitar chopping on the offbeat.
beats.after: Millie Small's "My Boy Lollypop" of 1964 was Jamaica's first international hit. In 1965 and 1966, as American soul grew slower and smoother, ska slowed with it into rocksteady. In the late 1970s, bands around Coventry joined ska rhythms to punk guitar in the 2 Tone style.

soul.hook: Soul joined gospel to rhythm and blues: Sam Cooke left a gospel group for secular music, and Aretha Franklin began as a gospel singer. From a converted photography studio in Detroit, Motown put 79 songs in the Billboard top ten in the 1960s, and funk followed.

beats.before: Soul grew out of African-American gospel music and rhythm and blues, joining their religious and secular styles in the 1950s. Ray Charles began a run of hits with "I Got a Woman" in 1954.
beats.who: Sam Cooke sang lead in the gospel group the Soul Stirrers before he moved into secular music. In Detroit, Berry Gordy founded Tamla Records, later Motown, on 12 January 1959. He turned a photography studio at 2648 West Grand Boulevard into a recording studio and office. Aretha Franklin, first a gospel singer, began making secular records in 1960 and later recorded for Atlantic.
beats.why: Motown, an African American-owned label, won white listeners as well. Between 1960 and 1969, 79 Motown songs reached the Billboard top ten.
beats.after: James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone moved on into funk. Neo soul, drawing on hip-hop, grew from it around 1994.

spirituals.hook: Spirituals were first sung in secret meetings by enslaved people in the American South; the first collection was printed in 1867. Nine students, the Fisk Jubilee Singers, took them to the White House by 1872, and blues and gospel grew from them.

beats.before: Spirituals grew from African musical traditions blended with Christian hymns brought by missionaries and slaveholders to enslaved Africans in the American South.
beats.who: The songs first flourished in secret meetings, the hush harbors, and later spread to camp meetings and revivals. The first collection came in 1867, when the abolitionists Charles Pickard Ware, Lucy McKim Garrison and William Francis Allen printed Slave Songs of the United States, with songs Ware took down from the Gullah people of South Carolina's Port Royal Islands.
beats.why: On 6 October 1871 nine students of the new Fisk school in Nashville, Tennessee, set out as the Fisk Jubilee Singers to raise money for it. At first they left out the slave songs, sacred to their parents; then the Reverend Alexander Reid gave them "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot", learned from Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved by the Choctaw. By 1872 they sang at the White House, and in 1873 they toured Europe.
beats.after: Blues and gospel grew from the spirituals, and civil rights freedom songs such as "Oh, Freedom!" were adapted from them.

swing.hook: Swing took off at the Palomar Ballroom on 21 August 1935, when young white dancers took to Benny Goodman's band, playing arrangements bought from Fletcher Henderson, whose own band the Depression had closed. Its small jump bands led to rhythm and blues, and its players worked out bebop.

beats.why: The Great Depression put Henderson's band out of business in 1934. Henderson then sold arrangements to the bandleader Benny Goodman. beats.after: Small bands led by Louis Jordan and Lucky Millinder played a jump swing that led to rhythm and blues. In 1940 Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and others whom swing had brought to New York began to work out bebop.

tango.hook: Tango's first known group was two Afro-Argentine musicians playing in Buenos Aires from the early 1870s, and in 1903 "El Choclo" had to be recorded in Paris because Argentina had no studios. In the 1950s Ástor Piazzolla rebuilt it from jazz and classical elements.

beats.before: Tango grew from the payada, the milonga of the Argentine and Uruguayan pampas, and Uruguayan candombe, which is believed to have been practised in Argentina since the first enslaved Africans were brought there.
beats.who: The first tango group was two Afro-Argentines, Casimiro Alcorta on violin and Sinforoso on clarinet, who played small concerts in Buenos Aires from the early 1870s to the early 1890s.
